articles.title: 'Cancer treatment plummeted me into menopause'
articles.summary: Women are calling for more support to deal with menopause caused by their cancer treatment.
articles.body:
Before her diagnosis in 2022, Jo, now 55, from East Yorkshire, had been taking hormonal replacement therapy (HRT) to manage the menopause.

Part of her treatment included surgery, which meant she had to stop taking HRT, and is still unable to use it.

"For me personally, my menopause symptoms came back with a vengeance almost immediately," she says.

"As well as recovering from surgery, which is quite gruelling, to then be mixed with hot flushes, aching limbs, brain fog, up and down emotions - I felt like I'd gone back about 10 years."

According to the NHS , menopause is when your periods stop due to lower hormone levels, and symptoms usually begin between the ages of 45 and 55.

However, people can experience menopause earlier or at an increased rate.

This can be brought on by a number of factors, including certain hormone medicines, ovarian surgery or treatment for some types of cancer.

Chemotherapy, pelvic radiotherapy, stem cell transplantation and surgery can all trigger menopause, on a temporary or permanent basis.

Jo and others say they were not prepared for this aspect of their treatment's side effects, and are calling for greater awareness and support to be made available.

"You're battling at the time with the diagnosis and the treatment and the surgery and how that's going to impact you," Jo explains.

"I never in my life thought that it would impact my menopause and it was never discussed. So it was a bit of a shock."

The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) said its National Cancer Plan would ensure patients had a personalised plan "so the long-term effects of treatment, including menopause, are recognised and built into their ongoing care".

Jo volunteers with Menopause and Cancer, a non-profit which advocates for accessible services for patients navigating the menopause after cancer.

She helps to run a support group in York, and calls it "life-changing and life-affirming in the same breath" to find a community of others in a similar position.

"You suddenly find this pocket of people that you can completely relate to.

"Because I didn't have a great experience, I feel I can support those that are in an earlier stage than me, so that they get the support even if I didn't."

Any information offered should be available from the start of someone's treatment journey and tailored to each individual, she adds.

"Everyone's experience with menopause is different.

"Having a toolkit signposting services that could be relevant for you and then you are empowered to pick the ones that suit you, that would be the perfect scenario."

Like Jo, Claire Hurst was already experiencing menopausal symptoms when she was diagnosed with breast cancer at 50.

As part of her treatment, she was given medication that rapidly put her in a medically-induced menopause, which she describes as "really, really challenging".

"There is no gradual shift. There's no time to adjust," she says.

"You are literally plummeted into the menopause."

She praises the "exceptional" healthcare support she received from the oncology team but says she felt left to manage the menopause on her own.

"Nobody sits you down and says, 'by the way, this is going to be probably the toughest part of your journey'."

Now 53, Claire is the founder of the Rebalance Clinic in Addingham, West Yorkshire.

She works with women experiencing the menopause, including those undergoing or recovering from breast cancer treatment.

For her, helping to connect patients with the relevant information and services should involve "joined-up thinking" between different organisations.

"Post treatment, there [should be] some follow-on programme where you are able to access really good resources," she says.

"When you educate, you empower. When people understand what's happening, they then go, 'okay, so it's not just me'.

"I think the biggest part for anybody going through the menopause is you are presented with a body that feels and works very, very differently."

Danni Binnington, founder of Menopause and Cancer, says the abrupt shift to menopause during or after treatment is what can be jarring for many.

"What we hear is people feel very lonely, very desperate. They say navigating menopause after cancer is actually worse than the cancer treatment," she says.

Information and advice about what patients could experience should be provided alongside other oncology services, according to her.

The community interest company (CIC) is calling for more information about the possible impacts of cancer treatment, through its Call for Change campaign.

A 2025 survey conducted by the CIC found out of 1,300 respondents, less than half were aware that their particular cancer treatment could induce menopause.

98% said they felt there should be more support from healthcare professionals for menopause following treatment.

"Knowledge is power and the last thing you want is to sit in this big black hole - and that is what people tell us they experience at the moment," Binnington adds.

"What we need to do is we need to bring it out into the open, we need to talk about it, we need to inform people, and then we need to signpost to services to help."

A DHSC spokesperson said: "No woman should feel left without support after cancer treatment, and we recognise the impact that treatment-induced menopause can have, both physically and emotionally.

"Through our National Cancer Plan, we will ensure every cancer patient has a personalised cancer plan and a named clinical nurse specialist, so the long-term effects of treatment, including menopause, are recognised and built into their ongoing care."

The government's Renewed Women's Health Strategy also focused on menopause as "a core priority", they added.

articles.title: How a hit-and-run led to a labour of love for maps artist
articles.summary: Joshua Tabti took up cartography in 2019 while housebound - and now calls it his career.
articles.body:
"I really wanted to draw a map of Iceland, where I used to live - I worked there for a year as a glacier guide," explains the 32-year-old from his studio on a drizzly Tuesday afternoon.

Unable to continue in his job as a climbing instructor due to his injuries, Joshua found a new purpose in cartography, which has since become his career.

"Making maps is the main passion. I studied art at university. I also really love geography, language and history," he says.

"I get to combine all of them in one, so it's a real passion."

Joshua's latest project - painstakingly researched over two months before it was carefully crafted with dip pen and ink - is a map of Yorkshire and Lancashire inspired by those produced by Lord of the Rings author JRR Tolkien.

He says: "A map of Yorkshire is something I have wanted to tackle for a couple of years, so I have slowly been researching it and trying to gather a database of all the locations and particularly the hidden gems that I wouldn't to be able to find online.

"It's been a bit of a bigger project than I expected. Going from coast to coast also includes Lancashire, so there was much more research that went into it."

Joshua spends roughly half of his time on a project completing research before the intricate process of drawing begins.

"It's a lot of careful inkwork," he admits.

Any errors involve "a lot of rubbing out", or shaving off the top layer of paper.

Joshua also sought the input of local residents on an online forum for his latest piece of work to help refine the project.

"To me it's really important that the landscapes are very recognisable to a local," he says.

"It's a great way to fill in any gaps. It's really encouraging to read comments from people and I think the thing that matters most is that people feel represented, or when someone recognises the details and all the effort.

Hertfordshire-based Joshua estimates he has now made about 30 pictorial maps, depicting landscapes as diverse as the island of Ireland, Malaysia and Virginia.

"In medieval times people would draw the landscape from an oblique angle, I have really enjoyed bringing to life that old tradition."

"I grew up in High Wycombe and had no real idea as a child that we were actually that close to London," he recalls.

"We would just go on picnics and to the countryside. It was a friend at school that introduced me to the books. Those stories became a symbol for home in a way, and friendship.

"That sort of stuff is quite a big theme in the books. The maps fascinated me as a boy, as a teenager."

His labour of love, born out of misery, has also led to the discovery of new places.

"That's the pleasure because I get to learn so much about a location, its culture, its history.

"I really enjoy visiting through the pen."

One such location was the French Alps, which had been next on his list of places to visit prior to being hit by a car while cycling in south London.

"To finally visit and see the landscapes I had known so well from drawing them, but had never stayed in, that was a real pleasure.

"The blessing in disguise was that it [the crash] got me back into illustration and art.

"That was a silver lining of a rubbish accident."

articles.title: Alexander brothers allegedly paid for coverage of sex-trafficking trial as writers deny favorable treatment
articles.summary: The Alexander brothers each received 30 years in prison, but allegations that they paid journalists for favorable trial coverage add a new twist.
articles.body: The Alexander brothers allegedly paid independent journalists for writing favorable coverage of their sex-trafficking trial – claims those writers have denied – as the wealthy trio sought to beat the federal charges before they were convicted and sentenced. Tal Alexander, 40, and his 39-year-old twin brothers, Oren and Alon Alexander, were convicted in March of conspiracy to commit sex crimes, including with minors. They each were sentenced on Oct. 27 to 30 years in prison. The jet-setting trio was found guilty of working together and with others to engage in sex trafficking, including by repeatedly drugging, sexually assaulting and raping numerous female victims. Now, the brothers face civil litigation from women who say they were victims. PRIVATE JETS, YACHTS AND POWERFUL FRIENDS HELPED ALEXANDER BROTHERS LURE WOMEN — AND SILENCE THEM, LAWYER SAYS But two independent journalists who covered the proceedings also are facing accusations. Daniel Mael is one of two writers accused in a New York Times piece of accepting payment to portray the trio of brothers in a positive way. But that’s not true, Mael said in a phone call with Fox News Digital. He simply wrote about his own conclusions, he said. Mael rejected claims from the New York Times report that he was paid $15,000 for writing "sympathetic posts" about the brothers during their trial. In the report, publisher Frank Parlato was said to have been paid $10,000 for similar writings. Mael declined to discuss the details of his financial agreement with the Alexanders’ publicist, Juda Engelmayer. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Engelmayer "offered to help subsidize part of the cost of covering the case, and I accepted," Mael wrote in a statement on X on Nov. 5. "No one requested favorable coverage, no one dictated a single word, and no one exercised the slightest editorial influence over my reporting." Parlato also declined to discuss whether he was paid for his writing. In an email to Fox News Digital, he maintained his coverage was independent. "I have never spoken to the Alexander brothers," Parlato wrote. "Nobody tells me what to write. Nobody sees my stories before publication. "I wrote about the brothers from court records, before trial, when they were presumed innocent. I write what I believe is true." SEND US A TIP "By the time the Alexander brothers went to trial, they had already been convicted in the court of public opinion," Engelmayer told Fox News Digital in an email. "The coverage was extensive, overwhelmingly negative, and largely driven by the allegations against them. There was very little interest in examining anything that might challenge the prevailing narrative." To make sure the defense's perspective "was at least heard," he contacted independent journalists who might be willing to cover the trial, he said. He sought those who would ask "the questions that weren't being asked elsewhere." Mael published frequent trial updates on his Substack. And sometimes, he presented evidence that weakened the defense’s case. A text from Alon Alexander referencing how he "took down a 17 year old," was "perhaps the most damning piece of evidence," Mael wrote in a recap of the trial’s eighth day. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST He bristled at the New York Times’ suggestion that he covered the trial with a bias against witnesses for the prosecution. "I never ever criticized the motives of the women on the stand," he said. "Ever." Mael asserted that his writing was independent and accurate, even though it was supported financially by Engelmayer. Parlato’s online platform, The Frank Report, published articles suggesting the Alexanders’ innocence in July and August 2025. One of the published pieces, "What If Everything You’ve Been Told About the Alexander Brothers Case Is Wrong? And Other Matters," was written by Engelmayer. Brothers on trial The Alexander brothers grew up in a wealthy Miami family. Oren and Tal were star real-estate agents who sold palatial homes to celebrities and the ultra-wealthy in New York, Miami, Aspen and beyond. Alon worked as an executive at the family’s Miami-based private security company, Kent Security. Their lifestyle put them on private jets and super yachts, and at exclusive parties. And they used that world as a hunting ground, prosecutors said. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS The brothers, who resided primarily in New York and Miami, Florida, used their "wealth and prominence to create and facilitate opportunities to sexually assault women," according to the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York. For years, they identified women through dating apps, clubs, parties and promoters, then lured them with trips, luxury accommodations, and access to powerful people and Hollywood celebrities. Once the women were isolated, the brothers drugged them and sexually assaulted them—sometimes together or with other men. In some cases, they recorded the attacks. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB Eleven women testified at their trial. Prosecutors said more than 70 women came forward with similar accounts. With the criminal proceedings finalized, three women are pursuing civil cases against the trio of brothers. GOT A TIP? At sentencing in their criminal trial, the brothers denied drugging, raping or trafficking anyone. But they did express regret over their past behavior. Prosecutors sought life in prison. The defense had asked for the 15-year minimum sentence. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL Judge Valerie Caproni also imposed 10 years of supervised release on each brother, with fines of $300,000 for Alon and Oren and $350,000 for Tal. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Alexanders’ attorney did not respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

articles.title: An elderly Florida homeowner suing his insurer over sewage damage broke his leg when his wheelchair flipped outside the courthouse, and the trial went ahead without him; an appeals court has now ordered a new trial
articles.summary: A trip to the court house that was expected to bring an elderly Florida homeowner closer to resolving a long running insurance dispute ended in a medical
articles.body: A trip to the court house that was expected to bring an elderly Florida homeowner closer to resolving a long running insurance dispute ended in a medical emergency. The homeowner broke his leg and had to have surgery after his wheelchair tipped over in the courthouse parking lot, and so he couldn’t participate in his own trial. He did not attend, but the trial went ahead and he was found against by the jury. But a Florida appeals court has now overturned that verdict, ordering a new trial and raising important questions about a policy exclusion used by property insurers.Verdict turns around in wheelchair accidentFlorida’s Second District Court of Appeal overturned the jury’s verdict on September 25, finding that the trial court erred in allowing the case to proceed after the homeowner was seriously injured, Insurance Business reported.The accident happened outside the courthouse when his wheelchair rolled across the parking lot, hit the bumper of a car and tipped over. The fall broke his tibia and ankle and he was unable to attend the proceedings or testify.The homeowner was an elderly fellow who had had a stroke the prior year. He was also preparing for surgery after the accident. His lawyer told the court of the emergency the morning after jury selection began April 28, 2025, in Pinellas County.The homeowner’s attorney and Universal Property & Casualty Insurance Company requested a mistrial. But the judge denied the requests and let the case proceed without the homeowner.The appeals court later ruled that the denial of his right to be present at and participate in his own trial was a fundamental error. It pointed out the significance of a party’s right to participate in proceedings and sent the matter back for a new trial.Dispute over insurance dates back to 2019The heart of the dispute involves water and sewage damage from a 2019 plumbing failure at the homeowner’s property.The property’s cast-iron plumbing system failed, causing sewage and water to spread across the floors, Insurance Business reported. The homeowner subsequently filed a claim with her insurer to pay for the removal and replacement of sections of the house so that the damaged pipes could be accessed and repaired.Universal Property & Casualty Insurance Company denied part of the claim, and the homeowner sued.In the first trial, the jury ultimately found that the claimed losses were excluded under the insurance policy. The appeals court has now overturned that decision, meaning the coverage dispute will have to be re-considered.Neglect exclusion throws up wider insurance issuesIn addition to the procedural issue, the case has also drawn attention to how insurers understand policy exclusions dealing with the upkeep of property.A concurring opinion questioned Universal’s reliance on a neglect exclusion, according to Insurance Business. The provision requires that the policyholder take reasonable steps to protect and preserve his property at and after a loss.The insurer argued that there was a prior loss in the form of a plumbing backup in 2016 or 2017. Universal said the exclusion applied because the homeowner had only replaced toilets, not made more extensive plumbing repairs.But the concurring judge challenged this interpretation, saying the provision relates to acts committed during or following a loss, not failures before it.The opinion also noted concern that accepting the insurer’s view could effectively force homeowners to replace entire plumbing systems after relatively minor incidents in an effort to protect their future coverage.What the ruling means for insurersThe appeals court ordered a new trial, but the basic coverage dispute is still unresolved. The view may be subject to change prior to formal release.If the logic behind the negligence exclusion stands, the decision could affect how Florida property insurers consider past maintenance problems in deciding whether to pay claims for subsequent damage.Images Courtesy: istockYou use AI every day. articles.title: After more than 400 trees were cut at Trump's Washington golf course, a federal judge names a former prosecutor to investigate whether government lawyers misled her about plans to continue redevelopment
articles.summary: A dispute over a public golf course in the heart of Washington DC has taken an unexpected turn, moving beyond questions of landscaping and redevelopment
articles.body: A dispute over a public golf course in the heart of Washington DC has taken an unexpected turn, moving beyond questions of landscaping and redevelopment to the conduct of the federal government itself. What began as a legal challenge to President Donald Trump's plans to transform a historic recreational space has now prompted a judicial investigation into whether government lawyers misrepresented the administration's intentions. With hundreds of trees already removed and construction plans facing resistance, the case has become a test of how far the government can go when a court has ordered it to stop.Former prosecutor appointed to examine government conductAccording to the latest report by Reuters, US District Judge Ana Reyes announced on Saturday that she would appoint Jessie Liu, a former US attorney for the District of Columbia, as a special master to investigate whether lawyers representing the Justice and Interior departments committed ethical violations during the proceedings.The appointment follows a hearing on October 30, when Reyes raised concerns that government attorneys may have misrepresented the administration's plans to proceed with renovations at East Potomac Golf Links. The judge had previously issued an order temporarily blocking aspects of the redevelopment, but Trump subsequently indicated that work would begin immediately.Reuters also reported that Reyes was particularly concerned about the apparent contradiction between the president's public statements and the assurances presented by government lawyers in court. The judge had also expressed reservations about being asked to disregard the president's own announcements.The Guardian report states that Liu will examine the conduct of officials and legal representatives involved in the case, including those from the Department of Justice, Interior Department and National Park Service. The judge is allowing both sides to submit written responses to her proposed appointment before the next scheduled hearing.The controversy surrounding the tree removalAt the centre of the dispute is East Potomac Park, a historic public recreational area situated along the Potomac River. The Trump administration intends to close the golf course and park on November 15 as part of its redevelopment plans.The proposed transformation involves creating what the administration describes as a championship-level golf destination capable of hosting major tournaments and other significant sporting events, states the Guardian report.However, the project has faced opposition from preservation advocates and local residents. A lawsuit filed in February by the DC Preservation League and two Washington residents challenges the proposed reconstruction, arguing that it violates environmental protections and congressional legislation governing the preservation of the historic park.As The Guardian reported, more than 400 trees were cut down during the early stages of the controversy, raising questions about whether officials had proceeded with work despite assurances given to the court.Reyes subsequently issued an injunction temporarily preventing the government from removing or damaging additional trees. The order also requires the administration to provide 10 days' written notice before undertaking any irreversible changes to the golf course's existing features while the litigation continues.Why Jessie Liu's appointment mattersLiu brings considerable experience in federal law enforcement and the Justice Department. During Trump's first presidential term, she served as the US attorney for the District of Columbia, overseeing several high-profile matters referred to her office during special counsel Robert Mueller's investigation into alleged Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election, states Reuters report.She also supervised the criminal case involving Roger Stone, Trump's longtime friend and political adviser. Trump later nominated Liu for the position of associate attorney general, one of the Justice Department's senior leadership roles, although she eventually withdrew after encountering opposition in the Senate, the latest report claims.The Guardian noted that appointing a special master to investigate the conduct of participants in a court case is a significant development. Legal experts have suggested that such an investigation could potentially precede contempt-of-court proceedings, depending on what the inquiry establishes.A wider political and legal confrontationThe Interior Department has criticised Reyes's intervention, describing her as politically motivated and accusing her of obstructing the president's efforts to improve Washington's appearance, Reuters reported.The golf course redevelopment is part of Trump's broader effort to reshape the capital through architectural and construction projects. However, the dispute has placed the administration's approach to public land, environmental safeguards and compliance with judicial orders under scrutiny.For Reyes, the immediate question is whether government representatives accurately communicated the administration's intentions and complied with the court's directions. The investigation will now seek to establish who authorised the disputed work, what assurances were given and whether those assurances were truthful.What remains a relatively modest golf course redevelopment project has consequently developed into a much larger legal confrontation, with its outcome potentially carrying implications beyond the future of East Potomac Park.Images Courtesy: Instagram/realdonaldtrump and Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APYou use AI every day. articles.title: Props used in films at Buckinghamshire company up for auction
articles.summary: Among the items are the olive tree from the set of the Abba musical and yew trees from a 007 film.
articles.body:
Props used in James Bond films and the musical Mamma Mia! are up for auction on Monday.

For the past 35 years, Living Props in Iver Heath, Buckinghamshire has worked on some of the world's best-known films and television productions.

The business, located near Pinewood Studios, was founded in 1991 by Brian Maslin, who was later joined by his son Blake, and Mick Lambert.

It is now closing and selling its stock including props, statues and benches as well as selected plants and specimen trees through an online auction .

Brian said he was sad to be leaving it all behind, but "we are leaving at the top of our game".

Giving the reasons for closing, he said that a company was keen to buy the site and work was now coming "in fits and starts" - either very busy or very quiet.

One of the most recognisable pieces in the sale is an olive tree that appeared in Mamma Mia!

The Greek village in the musical was recreated inside Pinewood Studios' famous 007 Stage, with the olive tree positioned at the top of the village.

"The designer came up to me and she said 'but we want big branches on it. We want to be able to dance underneath the tree'," Brian remembered.

"And I said 'well, olives don't do that'."

However, Brian and his team fitted metal girdles around the trunk, supporting additional branches and foliage to create a wide canopy.

This allowed the cast to dance beneath the tree, while the lighting department could position lights within its branches.

During the filming of the Bond film No Time to Die, Brian was tasked with creating a house and garden on a frozen lake in Norway.

"But it wasn't the normal Norway winter and the ice started melting and the house started slipping off the ice," he recalled.

The Living Props team brought fresh snow down from the mountains by the digger-load to maintain the winter setting.

Among the other pieces coming to auction are three cloud-pruned yew trees, originally purchased as part of a group of four for the James Bond film Die Another Day.

They stood either side of a pair of imposing gates in a Japanese garden set, as a hovercraft came "hurtling towards these two big doors," said Blake.

Brian said that AI and CGI would "naturally make inroads into the industry" but at the end of the day actors liked working with physical props and scenery as they "felt more at home".

articles.title: In the UK, a developer and four linked firms have been ordered to pay £46.5 million towards fire-safety work on seven Manchester buildings, following a landmark tribunal ruling that cut the government's claim
articles.summary: Manchester property developer Urban Splash and four companies linked to it have been ordered to pay £46.5 million towards essential fire safety repairs at
articles.body: Manchester property developer Urban Splash and four companies linked to it have been ordered to pay £46.5 million towards essential fire safety repairs at seven residential developments across the city. The ruling was made by the First-tier Tribunal (Property Chamber) after a legal case brought by the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government. The government had originally sought to recover more than £60 million spent or set aside to replace dangerous cladding and fix internal building defects across the sites. The tribunal agreed that more than £60.6 million worth of work was reasonably needed. However, the panel reduced the final amount to reflect wider failures by the government and regulators, which were highlighted by the Grenfell Tower Inquiry. The decision is one of the largest amounts the government has recovered under powers introduced by the Building Safety Act 2022.The order means Urban Splash Limited, Urban Splash Developments Limited, Urban Splash Group Holdings Limited, Urban Splash Work Limited and Stubbs Mill LLP must share responsibility for the payment. Most of the money will go towards repaying the government's Building Safety Fund. A further £741,594 will be paid to the management company of one of the residential developments. Four other companies named in the original case, including external investment funds, were not ordered to pay. The panel decided that making them responsible would not be fair or reasonable.Breakdown of the Manchester developmentsThe case involved seven residential developments built by Urban Splash in Manchester during the 2000s. Inspections carried out after the 2017 Grenfell Tower fire found serious construction and fire safety problems across the buildings. Inspectors found several types of defects. These included external cladding panels made from materials that could catch fire, missing or badly fitted cavity barriers, and damage to fire safety walls and floors designed to stop fires spreading between flats.The affected developments are located across several parts of the city. They include:Burton Place, CastlefieldChips Building, New IslingtonChristabel House, Dalton StreetEmmeline House, Dalton StreetSylvia House, Dalton StreetMoho Building, Ellesmere StreetThe Box Works, Worsley StreetThe tribunal held hearings over six weeks between April and July 2026. During the case, Urban Splash challenged the number and seriousness of the defects. The company also argued that the repair work paid for with public money had cost more than necessary. However, the tribunal rejected these arguments. It confirmed that £60,638,548, including VAT, had been reasonably spent or planned for essential repairs to make the buildings safe.Why the government claim was trimmedAlthough the government showed that the repair work was necessary, the tribunal decided not to award the full amount requested by ministers. The panel reduced the government's main claim by 10 per cent. It took into account past failures by public bodies responsible for overseeing building safety. The tribunal referred to findings from the Dame Judith Hackitt Review and the Grenfell Tower Inquiry. Both highlighted serious weaknesses in building rules, government guidance and systems for testing construction products in the UK. The panel made clear that the reduction did not mean ministers were being blamed for the physical defects in the buildings. Instead, it reflected the need to consider fairness when deciding how much developers should pay under section 124 of the Building Safety Act 2022. Housing Secretary Angela Rayner welcomed the main findings of the ruling and said the government would continue trying to recover public money spent on building safety work. "I welcome this important decision, which is clear that those responsible for unsafe buildings need to pay their fair share to fix them," Rayner said. "We will continue in our efforts to recover taxpayer funds spent on remediation and our work to make people's homes safe."Response from the developerFollowing the ruling, Urban Splash released a public statement describing the financial impact as significant. However, the company also said it wanted to work with government officials to find a way forward. "Our focus is firmly on the future rather than the past," the company said. "The challenges created by the Building Safety Act are not unique to Urban Splash. This is not simply about one company. It is about finding a way in which the objectives of building safety, housing delivery and regeneration can all be achieved together." The case could have an important effect on future building safety disputes across England. It provides a major example of how tribunals may decide how much developers must pay, whether parent companies can be held responsible and how the government can recover money spent on repairing unsafe buildings.You use AI every day. articles.title: Two arrested after police officers hurt in brawl outside Glasgow bare-knuckle fighting event
articles.summary: Police Scotland said three officers were hurt as they responded to reports of a large disturbance in streets close to the Ovo Hydro venue in Glasgow.
articles.body:
Two men have been arrested and three police officers injured during a street disturbance outside a bare-knuckle fighting championship in Glasgow.

Footage circulating on social media shows a group of men trading punches in the street outside the Ovo Hydro where the event was held on Saturday evening.

More than 20 police vehicles and a police helicopter converged on the area. Three officers were hurt, two of them requiring medical treatment, as they responded to the disorder.

Police Scotland said two men, aged 32 and 27, had been arrested and charged with offences including assault, obstructing police and threatening and abusive behaviour.

Thousands of spectators had earlier gathered for the Bare Knuckle Fighting Championship (BKFC) event where Sean Weir from Wishaw defeated Leigh Cohoon from Manchester when the referee stopped the fight in the first round.

At about 23:10, police said they received reports of a large disturbance in the Congress Road area outside the venue.

Ch Insp Paul Daley said: "Several officers were assaulted whilst carrying out their duties during disorder following an event at the Hydro in Glasgow on Saturday night.

"Violence against officers is disgraceful and will not be tolerated. Being assaulted is not part of the job and it's extremely fortunate they were not seriously injured."

The two men who have been charged are expected to appear at Glasgow Sheriff Court on Monday.

A third man was arrested and issued with a recorded police warning.

Police said inquiries were continuing and that anyone found responsible "will be brought to justice".

They have asked anyone with information about the disturbance to contact them.

articles.title: West Virginia Supreme Court reverses $31,054 divorce payout tied to rise in value of house bought before marriage; wife remains entitled to a share of mortgage principal reduction
articles.summary: The West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals has overturned a lower court decision that ordered a man to pay his former wife $31,054 for the increase in
articles.body: The West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals has overturned a lower court decision that ordered a man to pay his former wife $31,054 for the increase in market value of a home he bought before their marriage. The decision, in the case of Shawn H. v. Elise H., makes clear that any increase in the market value of a property bought by one spouse before marriage remains that person's separate property. The other spouse can only claim a share of that increase if they prove their own work directly helped raise the property's value. Although the Supreme Court overturned the payment linked to the home's overall increase in market value, it confirmed that the former wife is still entitled to a fair share of the financial value gained through mortgage principal payments made during the marriage. The ruling explains how West Virginia courts must separate property owned before marriage from financial contributions made by both spouses during marriage when dividing assets in a divorce.Background of the premarital home disputeThe case involved a house that Shawn H. bought before marrying Elise H. Since the property was purchased before the marriage, it remained legally registered in the husband's name alone. After the couple married and later divorced, the family court looked at how the home's financial value had changed during the years they lived together. During the first divorce proceedings, the lower court decided that the increase in the home's market value during the marriage should count as marital property. This meant it could be shared between the former spouses. The court ordered the husband to pay the wife $31,054 as her share of the increase in the property's value. The husband challenged the decision. He argued that the home's value had increased because of wider changes in the property market, not because of money spent during the marriage or improvements made by his former wife.Legal distinction between passive and active appreciationWhile reviewing the case under docket number 24-673, the West Virginia Supreme Court examined the state laws that explain the difference between separate and marital property under West Virginia Code § 48-1-237. Under West Virginia law, property bought by someone before marriage is treated as separate property. Any increase in its value during the marriage also remains separate, unless the other spouse can show that shared marital money or significant personal work directly caused the increase. The Supreme Court explained the difference between two types of property value increases. Passive appreciation happens when a property's value rises because of general market conditions. Active appreciation happens when its value increases because of renovations, improvements or financial contributions. In this case, there was not enough evidence to show that the former wife's work or money from the marriage had directly increased the home's market value beyond the rise caused by general property market trends. The justices therefore ruled that the lower court had made a legal error by awarding her a share of the home's overall increase in value.Entitlement to mortgage principal reductionAlthough the Supreme Court removed the $31,054 payment for the increase in market value, it agreed that the former wife was still entitled to a share of the financial value created by paying down the mortgage during the marriage. Under earlier West Virginia court decisions, when a couple uses their shared income during marriage to make mortgage payments on a home owned by one spouse before marriage, the reduction in the original loan amount creates a financial interest for the marital estate. The justices explained that the house itself remains the separate property of the spouse who owned it before marriage. However, any increase in the couple's financial equity that comes from using shared earnings to reduce the mortgage principal must be worked out and fairly divided during the divorce. "We remand this matter for the family court to determine the marital interest resulting from the parties' financial contributions toward the reduction of the mortgage principal during the marriage and to equitably distribute that interest," the opinion stated. The case will now return to the lower family court. It must calculate the exact amount each former spouse is entitled to receive based only on the reduction in the mortgage principal paid during the marriage.You use AI every day. articles.title: A North Dakota woman spent more than $110,000 on purchases for a house she built with her partner on land held by his family trust; after they split, a court rejected her claim for the home's improvements
articles.summary: A North Dakota woman who spent more than $110,000 on building materials and other items for a home on land owned by her longtime partner's family trust
articles.body: A North Dakota woman who spent more than $110,000 on building materials and other items for a home on land owned by her longtime partner's family trust cannot get her money back through an unjust enrichment claim, the North Dakota Supreme Court has ruled. The decision, issued on Friday, 6 November 2026, upheld a Grant County District Court ruling that rejected a financial claim filed by Mary Roth. She had sought repayment after her relationship with rancher Gary Meyer ended. The case involved a 10-acre residential property in rural Grant County, North Dakota, where the couple lived and ran a cattle business together. Gary Meyer had lived on the property for decades and believed he owned it. However, the legal ownership belonged to the Jean L. Ehrmantrout Residuary Trust, which was managed by his three sons as co-trustees. After the relationship ended, Roth asked to be repaid for the large number of items and materials she bought to build and improve the home. She also filed an unjust enrichment claim against the trust's beneficiaries, arguing that they had unfairly benefited from her spending.Proof of spending is not proof of added valueWriting for the unanimous Supreme Court, Justice Jon J. Jensen explained that showing how much money someone spent is not enough to win an unjust enrichment claim under North Dakota law. The court said these claims must focus on the actual financial benefit received by the property owner. They cannot be based only on the money spent by the person who bought the materials or paid for the work. "Receipts and a compilation of purchases show what Mary Roth spent; they do not show the value those purchases added to the property," Justice Jensen wrote in the opinion. Roth provided many receipts and financial records showing that she had spent more than $110,000. However, she did not provide expert evidence or property appraisals showing how much those purchases had actually increased the market value of the land owned by the family trust.Legal principle of unjust enrichmentUnder North Dakota law, a person making an unjust enrichment claim must prove five main things. First, the defendant received a benefit. Second, the person making the claim suffered a financial loss. Third, there must be a clear connection between that benefit and the financial loss. Fourth, there must be no valid reason for the benefit and loss to have occurred. Finally, there must be no other legal remedy available. The Supreme Court noted that the district court had accepted that Roth suffered a financial loss by paying for building materials and supplies for the home. However, there was not enough evidence to work out how much financial benefit the trust had received. The justices rejected the idea that purchase receipts or property listing prices could automatically be used to prove how much a property had gained in value. They said trial judges cannot simply estimate an increase in market value without proper evidence from property valuation experts. The court also referred to its 2018 decision in Tornabeni v. Wold. It repeated the legal principle that a person cannot receive compensation through an equity claim based only on money spent. They must also prove that the property owner received a clear and measurable financial benefit.End of lengthy multi-year litigationThe ruling on 6 November, issued under docket number 20260153, marks the third time the dispute between Roth and the Meyer estate has reached the North Dakota Supreme Court. The earlier appeals took place in 2024 and 2025. Chief Justice Lisa Fair McEvers, Justice Jerod E. Tufte, Justice Douglas A. Bahr and Justice Mark A. Friese all agreed with Justice Jensen's opinion. Their decision brings the long-running property dispute to an end. The Supreme Court upheld the Grant County District Court's third amended judgment. This means the property will remain with the family trust, and Roth will not receive the money she sought to recover.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: A young woman is warning other rideshare passengers after she says her Uber driver canceled a late-night trip while she was still inside the car. Elyse Madrid, 22, said she and a friend ordered an Uber at about 2:30 a.m. on a recent Saturday to travel from Chicago's Belmont Cragin neighborhood to a karaoke bar, according to CBS News Chicago. During the trip, Madrid noticed they did not appear to be heading in the right direction. Her concern grew when she said she watched the driver cancel the trip in the app while she and her friend were still sitting inside the vehicle. WOMAN'S ROUTINE UBER RIDE TAKES ALARMING TURN AFTER HER DRIVER MISSES THE EXIT Fox News Digital reached out to Madrid for comment. Uber told Fox News Digital that the driver in question has been removed from the platform while the incident is being investigated. "What has been reported is deeply distressing, and we have removed the driver's access to the Uber platform," an Uber spokesperson said. "We've reached out to police, and will support their investigation in any way we can." Madrid said she confronted the driver. She said he blamed the cancellation on problems with his phone and at one point claimed his sister had canceled the trip. "When we got out the car, he sped off like in a panic," Madrid said. She said the driver took off at about 40 to 50 mph. Madrid later filed a police report. The experience was particularly troubling for Madrid, who said she had been assaulted in a cab the previous August. Dillon Abend, the New Jersey-based founder and CEO of rideshare safety app 3rd-i, told Fox News Digital that passengers should speak up during a ride as soon as they notice something unusual. If the driver does not cooperate or if the passenger believes there is an immediate threat, he said people should call 911 and alert a trusted friend or family member. articles.title: ‘Giant step back in history’: Trump blames Democrats’ midterm sweep for $3 trillion market loss
articles.summary: US president Donald Trump has blamed the Democrats’ sweeping victory in the midterm elections for a $3 trillion wipeout in stock market value, saying
articles.body: US president Donald Trump has blamed the Democrats’ sweeping victory in the midterm elections for a $3 trillion wipeout in stock market value, saying America had “taken a giant step back in history” but promising that his party would return “bigger and stronger than ever before”.In a post on Truth Social, Trump said the market had suffered a one-day loss of $3 trillion despite having performed like a “rocketship” under his presidency.“America took a giant step back in History with the results of the last Election — Even the Stock Market, which has been a ‘ROCKETSHIP’ under ‘TRUMP,’ took a one day, 3 Trillion Dollar loss,” he wrote, before adding: “But have no fear, we will be back, BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE!”It was not the first time Trump had attributed the market decline to the Democratic victory. Speaking to reporters in Florida on Friday, he said the US had lost about $3 trillion after investors learnt that Democrats had performed well in the election, adding that the development was also linked to his administration’s position on Iran’s nuclear programme.“We lost about $3 trillion when they found out that the Democrats did well in the election, rather surprisingly, but that’s the way life goes. It had to do with the fact that we won’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon, so you always have to go with that first,” he said.At an appearance at Nasa’s Kennedy Space Centre on Friday, Trump again referred to the losses, suggesting he might have been more unhappy had the market gained the same amount.“Our country lost three trillion dollars all because of an election. I wonder what that means. If we would have gained three trillion dollars, I probably would have been more unhappy,” he said.The comments came after Wall Street experienced a sharp reversal following an initial rally on news of the Democratic sweep. On Wednesday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 1,569 points, or 3%, marking its strongest post-midterm election performance in 44 years. The S&P 500 gained 1.6%, with investors appearing to welcome the prospect of a divided government and more predictable policymaking.The mood changed sharply the following day. US stocks lost roughly $3 trillion in market value on Thursday, with the Nasdaq falling 5.2%, the S&P 500 dropping 3.8% and the Dow declining 2.9%, or more than 1,500 points, according to market reports.Technology and artificial intelligence-linked stocks bore the brunt of the sell-off. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell nearly 10% in intraday trading and briefly dropped as much as 11%. AMD and Micron each lost around 15%, while Nvidia fell almost 9%.The decline followed a sell-off in Asian markets, with South Korea’s Kospi falling 5.28%, Taiwan’s main index declining 3.2% and Japan’s Nikkei dropping 1.79%.While Trump linked the losses to the election result, market concerns also centred on the outlook for the technology sector, particularly the expansion of data centres. Several Democratic candidates campaigned on restricting or pausing new data centre projects, amid concerns about their demands on electricity grids and local infrastructure.In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican governor Greg Abbott after campaigning for an immediate moratorium on new data centres. Ohio’s Amy Acton and Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms also made restrictions on data centre development part of their campaigns.The political pushback has raised concerns among investors about permitting delays and the impact on companies involved in the AI infrastructure boom. Texas is a particular focus, with an estimated 27% of planned data centre capacity located in the state, according to Wells Fargo. Abbott had already paused new data centre permits in September pending an audit of the electricity grid.Trump’s remarks followed a historic setback for Republicans, with Democrats securing majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate. The result has shifted the balance of power in Washington and opened the door for Democrats to challenge the administration’s policies, scrutinise federal spending and launch investigations into the Trump administration.However, the Democratic gains do not mean the party will have an unrestricted legislative agenda. Trump retains the presidential veto, which allows him to block legislation passed by Congress unless lawmakers can secure a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override it.The president has already signalled that he is prepared to use the power. As the scale of the Democratic victory became clear, he posted a photograph of a red baseball cap bearing the word “VETO” on Truth Social.“It’s the power of veto. It’s one of the stronger powers that a president has,” Trump said after the Republican defeat.But Trump has also said he does not want to spend the next two years vetoing legislation. “I don't want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything,” he told Politico.The White House, for its part, appeared keen to remind Americans that the election result had not changed who occupies the Oval Office. After the Republican losses, its official X account posted: “PSA: TRUMP IS STILL YOUR PRESIDENT,” alongside a photograph of the president.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: New York turned part of Broadway into Times Square pedestrian plazas in 2009; months later, pedestrian injuries were down 35% and motorist injuries 63%
articles.summary: In 2009, New York transformed Times Square by closing part of Broadway to vehicles, resulting in a significant decrease in pedestrian and motorist injuries. Discover the long-term effects and benefits of this urban redesign.
articles.body: Anyone who has ever stood in Times Square probably knows the feeling. Crowds, noise, taxis, and a phone in every hand. In 2009, New York closed part of Broadway to cars and gave the space to people. The New York City Department of Transportation’s ‘Green Light for Midtown Evaluation Report,’ published in January 2010, said the number of pedestrian injuries in the project area dropped 35%. Driver and passenger injuries went down by 63%.Why Broadway needed a rethink Broadway runs through the street grid of Manhattan at an angle. Where it meets avenues, it creates busy junctions with multiple legs, and the crosswalks were long and confusing. According to the report, pedestrian accidents in Times Square were 137% more common than on other avenues in the neighbourhood. Times Square and Herald Square had ten times as many pedestrians as vehicles, thus making it easy for people to spill into the streets. The city announced its pilot project in February 2009. Broadway was closed to traffic on 24 May, and the construction was completed by the end of August. Crosswalks were shortened, traffic lanes became clearer, and plazas with seating took over road space. The first version used temporary materials and furnishings.What the numbers showedThe city used early police data to measure the results by comparing June through November 2009 with the same months in the three years before. Pedestrian injuries decreased by 35% in the project area. Herald Square saw a drop of 53%. Times Square was down by 40%. Driver and passenger injuries fell by 63%. However, not all groups saw such improvement. Cyclist injuries increased slightly, from an average of 11 injuries over those same June-November periods in the three years to 12 in 2009. The report also counted people walking in the street on one block of Seventh Avenue, between 45th and 46th streets. That figure dropped by 80%, from 5,025 to 1,022. The city also kept tabs on traffic. Northbound trips in West Midtown were 17% faster in autumn 2009 than in autumn 2008, according to taxi GPS data, while southbound trips were 2% slower. Field surveys showed longer cross-town travel times, but results varied a lot from street to street. There was little change in the total volume of traffic.Why people stayedFoot traffic in Times Square rose by 11%. The report says activities such as taking photos, checking maps and looking at billboards moved from the sidewalk into the new plazas. That left more room for people just trying to get places. The report cited a November 2009 survey by The Times Square Alliance that found 74% of New York City residents said the area had improved dramatically over the previous year. The transport department reviewed the safety, mobility and satisfaction results and recommended making the changes permanent. In February 2010, the mayor announced that the plazas would stay.How the idea spreadTimes Square was only the beginning. Hanife Vardi Topal and Karen A. Franck’s peer-reviewed study in The Journal of Public Space points out that Times Square Plaza was the first project of the city’s plaza programme, which the authors describe as the first of its kind in the US. The city's transportation department dates the programme's start to 2008, and it expanded citywide in 2009. By 2022, the transport department had listed 73 plazas as either completed or in progress. The authors studied five smaller plazas in Brooklyn and Queens, drawing on site observations, surveys, and interviews collected in 2018 and 2019. Four out of five were well-used. Plaza managers also described a shortage of funds for maintenance and events. The 2009 injury figures are early data, and they come from the city's own evaluation of its project. Still, Times Square suggests that giving space back to people can improve both safety and atmosphere.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Virginia redesigned Reston’s Lawyers Road after targeting a 20% crash reduction; after four lanes became two with turn and bike lanes, reported crashes fell from 16 to five a year
articles.summary: Discover how Virginia's road diet on Lawyers Road drastically reduced accidents by 69%, improved cyclist safety, and transformed community perceptions about road design.
articles.body: Sometimes the smartest way to fix a dangerous road might just be to take away space. That's what happened on Lawyers Road in Reston, Virginia. The 2015 National Roadway Safety Awards guide from the US federal Highway Administration (FHWA) says the Virginia Department of Transportation (VDOT) changed four lanes to two, put in a centre turn lane and made the extra width into bike lanes. VDOT announced the goal of reducing crashes by 20%. After the project, they fell from 16 a year to five, a drop of 69%.A busy road with a speeding problem Lawyers Road is two miles long, approximately three kilometres. The number of vehicles using this road was 10,000 per day before the changes. According to the guide, the road is noted for speeding problems, and it experiences an average of 16 accidents per year. The layout didn't help much. On a four-lane road with no divider, fast-through traffic shares the inside lane with drivers waiting to turn left. Such roads, the document adds, tend to have relatively higher accident rates. Imagine a corridor where some people are running past, and some are suddenly stopping to turn. This situation here was similar.How a road diet works The fix was called a road diet. Nobody loses weight; the road just gets narrower. Four lanes of traffic on Lawyers Road were reduced to two with a centre lane for turning vehicles. There was also space for bike lanes. The work was little more than pavement markings, so VDOT added it to a resurfacing project already planned. FHWA’s write-up said that meant the cost to the state was minimal. VDOT also ran an enormous outreach effort, and it was during this effort that engineers publicly shared the 20% forecast.More than just fewer crashesThe crash drop wasn’t the only win. Speeds fell too. The average running speed decreased by 1 mph, which is about 1.6 km/h. However, the speeds of the fastest-moving traffic, where the drivers drove at least 5 mph (about 8km/h) faster than the speed limit, were significantly reduced. Cyclists got something too. The road got dedicated bike lanes and a signal that bicyclists can trigger, which the guide says has made biking safer. In short, the typical driver slowed down a little, but the riskiest speeding was almost gone.Residents came aroundNot everyone was sold at first. The idea was initially met with mixed support, which is to be expected when a road that people use every day suddenly changes. A VDOT survey showed a 74% approval rating after the project. The early concerns were resolved with the success of Lawyers Road. When nearby Soapstone Drive came up for resurfacing, many Reston residents supported a similar road diet. That project also gave positive results, the guide notes. Lawyers Road won the Infrastructure and Operational Improvement category of the 2015 awards, which FHWA and the Roadway Safety Foundation had jointly sponsored since 1998.Is this just a one-off?Not exactly, although Reston’s result was good. A 2010 FHWA study, ‘Evaluation of Lane Reduction “Road Diet” Measures on Crashes,’ examined 45 sites in California, Iowa, and Washington. Iowa sites saw a 47% dip in total crashes. In California and Washington, it dropped 19%. Together, the drop was 29%. Lawyers Road beat all of these figures. The same summary says that sites with smaller gains tended to have heavier traffic. This means that the benefits may dwindle as roads get busier. So, a road diet is not a magic fix, and one road cannot speak for all cities. However, it's a useful reminder: before widening a road, ask if a calmer layout could do the job.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: Panchmahal court sentences six, including five women, to 7 years for stripping and parading a 52-year-old woman naked over a family dispute; Rs 66,000 fine.
articles.body: Vadodara: In a chilling reminder of the cruelty that can unfold in the name of family honour, six persons, including five women, were sentenced to seven years in jail by a sessions court in Panchmahal on Saturday. They had stripped a 52-year-old woman and paraded her through her village in full public view.The disturbing incident took place in Feb 2024 in a village in Morva Hadaf taluka in Panchmahal district. Its roots lay in a young couple’s decision to elope. The woman’s son had entered into a relationship with a girl from the same village. This had enraged the girl’s family, whose members descended upon the young man’s parental home and unleashed their fury on his parents.“Both the father and the mother of the young man were severely assaulted. Five women from the girl’s family then stripped the 52-year-old mother and took her out in the village. They paraded her and later tied her to a tree with a rope. The incident had led to an outrage in the district,” said public prosecutor Rakesh Thakor.Following the incident, Panchmahal police registered a case against six accused on charges relating to outraging a woman’s modesty, using criminal force with the intent to disrobe her and wrongful confinement.After hearing the case, the sessions court found all six guilty and sentenced Shankar Valvai, Savita Valvai, Nanda Makwana, Sumitra Valvai, Kailas Valvai and Manjula Valvai to seven years of imprisonment. The court also imposed a collective penalty of Rs 66,000 on the convicts.Public prosecutor Thakor said sessions court judge Nipa Raval observed that such incidents had no place in society and could not be permitted.Meanwhile, there was a reconciliation in the family dispute that had triggered the violence. The eloped couple eventually returned to the village after their respective families reached a compromise and accepted their marriage. articles.title: Rajkot airport director’s stint lasts 23 days, transferred to Indore
articles.summary: AAI transfers Rajkot airport director Dhananjay Kumar Singh to Indore after 23 days; Sanjay Agrawal takes interim charge amid recent runway and maintenance incidents.
articles.body: Rajkot: Airports Authority of India (AAI) has transferred Rajkot airport director Dhananjay Kumar Singh to Indore airport, barely a month after he took charge.According to an official order issued by AAI headquarters on Nov 4, Sanjay Agrawal, joint general manager (CNS), was assigned the charge of airport director following Singh’s repatriation to parent cadre, directorate of commercial. An order issued by AAI on Nov 5 stated that Singh has been posted as director at Indore airport with immediate effect.At Rajkot, the new arrangement will continue until a regular incumbent is appointed or further orders are issued, the Nov 4 order stated.According to Rajkot airport sources, Singh took charge as airport director on Oct 12 on transfer from Jamnagar airport. His sudden transfer in less than a month’s time has surprised airport staff. While the official order does not specify any reason for his repatriation, employees have linked the move to two or three recent incidents at the airport.On Oct 28, firecrackers were burst near the runway to disperse birds and prevent bird hits. The exercise triggered a small fire in the grass near the runway, prompting authorities to divert a flight arriving from Delhi to another airport.
